title: All-IGZO monolithic memory: n-only periphery in the same tiers
idea: TRIZ #33 Homogeneity: build sense amps, decoders and drivers from the same IGZO transistors as the 2T0C array, using bootstrapped n-only (pseudo-CMOS) circuits, so each BEOL tier is a complete memory with no CMOS underneath. The whole stack can sit on any logic die's metal stack.
why: Fact 5 and 7: memory micrometres above compute (~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM) and periphery needs no separate FEOL; any logic fab's BEOL becomes DRAM capacity.

title: Polyploid bits: three tier copies charge-summed onto one bitline
idea: Heat-stressed plants often become polyploid, carrying extra genome copies; write each bit into three cells in three tiers on the same vertical bitline and activate all three together on read so their charges sum, letting one hot leaky tail cell be outvoted by the other two.
why: 125 C leakage tail: 3x summed signal that is statistically immune to single tail cells permits near-room-temperature refresh intervals in a dense 3D stack where tiers are cheap.

title: Redox-molecule monolayers in 3D capacitors hold charge for minutes
idea: Po: the capacitor is a molecule that refuses to give electrons back. Graft porphyrin or ferrocene redox monolayers inside porous 3D capacitor scaffolds so charge sits in discrete molecular oxidation states behind an activated electron-transfer barrier, giving minutes of retention without improving the access device.
why: Refresh skipped because retention exceeds data lifetimes; molecular charge density (~10-100 uC/cm2) also eases the charge wall (fact 1).

title: Swiss-roll DRAM: self-rolling nanomembrane turns one planar array into 50 tiers
idea: Scale jump from meter-scale battery jelly-rolls down to microns: fabricate a planar oxide-semiconductor 1T1C array on a pre-strained SiNx/SiNx bilayer, undercut it, and let the strain roll it into a ~10-um tube of ~50 windings; radial vias are electroplated afterwards through windows that line up after rolling. One lithography pass yields ~50 stacked tiers.
why: Attacks 3D's need for 26+ tiers and the litho cost of each tier (facts 2, 4): tier count comes from mechanics rather than deposition and etch loops, claiming ~20-50x bits per litho layer.

title: Brain-implant heat rule: DRAM-logic tile mosaic stitched by bonded bridges
idea: A brain implant may not warm tissue 1 C, so heat must never pool under memory; instead of stacking DRAM on hot logic, tile 1 mm DRAM and logic chiplets in a checkerboard mosaic and stitch adjacent edges with a hybrid-bonded bridge die carrying thousands of sub-100 um links. Every logic tile touches four DRAM tiles while no DRAM sits above a hotspot.
why: DRAM runs ~20-30 C cooler than HBM-on-logic, cutting refresh 4-8x (fact 3), with ~0.3 pJ/bit data movement (fact 5).

title: Holes drilled in a bulk dielectric block form inter-hole capacitors
idea: Po: the capacitor is a hole, not a pillar. Deposit a 3-5 um block of crystalline high-k (rutile TiO2 or doped ZrO2, k 40-80), drill a hexagonal hole array, and fill alternate holes with storage and plate electrodes so the dielectric is the solid wall between neighbouring holes instead of a 5 nm conformal ALD film.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): reaches the k~70 target in a matrix that cannot lean or collapse; wall thickness set by etch spacing rather than ALD conformality at extreme AR.

title: CCD imager registers: vertical charge-shift strings replace capacitors
idea: Adapted from CCD image sensors: a 3D gate stack wrapped around a vertical silicon or oxide-semiconductor channel stores bits as charge packets in potential wells under each gate tier; a read clocks packets down the string to a floating-diffusion sense node at the base, like a CCD vertical register.
why: Removes both 3D blockers, the capacitor and the lateral transistor (fact 2); ~4F2/N per bit with NAND-like one-litho-for-all-tiers cost; trade-off ~50-100 ns serial shift for 32-tier strings.

title: Pinned buried-well cells borrowed from image-sensor photodiodes
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying (from CMOS image sensors): store each bit as electrons in a fully depleted buried n-well capped by a p+ pinning layer, the trick that brings photodiode dark current to a few e-/s. A transfer gate dumps the packet onto a floating diffusion and source follower shared by 8 vertically stacked wells, read with correlated double sampling.
why: Fact 3: pinned surfaces cut generation leakage by orders of magnitude, so refresh could move from ms to seconds (refresh energy -90%+); no capacitor and one readout transistor per 8 bits.

title: Make the interposer the memory: DRAM-filled active interposer
idea: Swap substrate and memory roles: build the large silicon interposer under an accelerator (2,500+ mm2, relaxed 40-65 nm pitch, mostly empty silicon) as an 8-tier relaxed-pitch DRAM array with routing on top, so the accelerator sits directly on ~100 GB of memory with micron-scale vertical access.
why: Data movement and HBM tax (facts 5,6): turns wasted interposer area into memory at <1 pJ/bit, no TSV stack, made in mature-node fabs including U.S. ones.

title: Hexagonal 60-degree lattice replaces square grid for vertical-channel cells
idea: Substitute the orthogonal wordline/bitline grid with a triangular lattice: vertical-channel transistors at hexagonal close-packed sites defined by block-copolymer self-assembly, wordlines along one lattice direction and bitlines along a second at 60 degrees, so each cell occupies sqrt(3)/2*(2F)² = 3.46F² instead of 4F².
why: Litho-bound density (fact 4): ~13% more bits per area at the same F, a free 'half-node' without a new litho tool; hexagonal pillars also match the existing capacitor honeycomb.

title: Islamic-tiling artist's 60-degree lattice packs cells at 3.46F2
idea: A geometric-pattern artist would never use a square grid. Put vertical-channel cells on a triangular lattice, run wordlines along one 60-degree lattice direction and bitlines along a second, and pattern both with the periodic interference or spacer flows.
why: Hexagonal packing gives sqrt(3)/2 x 4F2 = 3.46F2, ~13% more bits per area beyond 4F2 with no node shrink (Facts 4, 7).

title: Complementary twin cells on adjacent tiers cancel stack variation
idea: Revive IBM's balanced-capacitor read-only store and early twin-cell DRAM: store each bit as opposite charges in vertically adjacent tiers on the same pillar and sense differentially, so tier-correlated etch and doping variation cancels and a ~1% single-ended raw BER becomes ~1e-6 at the pair.
why: Facts 1 and 2: Cs can drop ~2x and tiers can thin, since differential sensing doubles signal; relaxes the 3D capacitor requirement.

title: Bookshelf stacking: dies on edge with sidewall wiring, no TSVs
idea: Scale up from die to cube, reviving the 1990s Irvine Sensors cube: thin DRAM dies to 50 um, laminate 64 face-to-back, lap the stack edge, and metallize the exposed edge pads with 180-nm-class litho. The bus runs across the cube face to a logic die mounted perpendicular to the stack.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): reclaims ~30% of die area and the yield loss, using old tools in U.S. back-end lines.

title: Jeweler's plating bath: electroless cobalt wordline fill replaces tungsten
idea: The jeweler grows metal from a bath. Activate the lateral wordline cavities of a 3D stack with a Pd seed and fill them bottom-up with electroless Co-B or Ru at <=70C on a ~$100k wet bench.
why: Removes tungsten (China ~80%) and the $5M CVD-W chamber from array metallization. A 10-person team can qualify the bath chemistry.

title: Eliminate the capacitor: volatile charge-trap strings with ultrathin tunnel oxide
idea: Build a vertical NAND-style string, but with a ~1.5 nm tunnel oxide so electrons enter and leave a nitride trap layer by direct tunnelling in tens of ns (retention of seconds, refreshed like DRAM), avoiding Fowler-Nordheim wear-out.
why: Water: reuses the 3D NAND flow, where one deep-hole litho and clean sequence covers 100+ tiers; wet steps per bit fall >10x versus 1T1C DRAM. Endurance at 1e15 cycles is the key risk.

title: Eliminate etch-fill-polish cycles: flat-by-construction conversion patterning
idea: Define isolation and channels by locally converting silicon rather than removing it: patterned oxygen or nitrogen implant plus anneal (SIMOX-like) turns selected regions into insulator, so the surface stays planar and no gap-fill or CMP is needed.
why: Water: STI etch, fill, CMP and their cleans are among the heaviest UPW users per layer; a planar conversion flow removes them for the array, cutting array-module water ~10x.

title: Open-pit mine benches: one cone etch exposes every tier
idea: Borrowed from open-pit mining benches: instead of 3D-NAND-style resist-trim staircases (dozens of litho/trim cycles), one tapered isotropic etch cuts a conical pit through the whole 3D DRAM tier stack so every wordline tier surfaces as a concentric ring on the pit wall. Contacts land on the rings at radii set by cone angle and tier thickness, using a single contact mask.
why: Attacks 3D DRAM mask/capital cost (facts 2,4): replaces ~N/2 trim cycles with one etch; ring contacts wrap around the pit so staircase area falls ~3x and staircase process cost ~80% at 64+ tiers.

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM stacks with superconducting cuprate power and wordlines
idea: Po: memory lives in a freezer. Immerse accelerator memory stacks in LN2 at 77 K where access leakage falls >1e6x and retention exceeds hours so refresh is disabled, and use YBCO or Bi-2223 global wordlines and power grids so tall stacks avoid IR drop; one cryostat per AI rack.
why: Refresh zero plus ~2x mobility; cryocooler overhead (~10 W per W removed) only pays off in dense AI racks.

title: ZettaCore redox-molecule capacitors multiply charge per 3D node
idea: Revive ZettaCore's abandoned porphyrin memory: graft a monolayer of redox molecules onto each 3D cell's storage electrode so charge is held at discrete oxidation potentials (~10x areal charge versus a dielectric at the same voltage, multi-bit), accepting ~1% molecular-variation errors.
why: Fact 1: lifts the capacitor charge wall without AR 115 or k 70; short capacitors make 3D tiers practical.

title: Backside bitlines free the front side for capacitors alone
idea: IFR: 'bitlines occupy no space between capacitors.' Backward: build vertical-channel transistors and front-side capacitors, bond to a carrier, thin to the transistor bottoms and form bitlines on the wafer backside (borrowing backside-power-delivery flows), so no bitline contact threads between capacitor pillars.
why: Density and litho (facts 1, 4): 4F2 with relaxed capacitor spacing, ~30-40% lower bitline coupling, and one fewer EUV contact layer.

title: In-stack gain tiers segment vertical bitlines every 32 tiers
idea: Worse: hang 300 tiers of cells on one vertical bitline so its capacitance buries the signal and forces a sense amp per short column. Flip: insert a 'gain tier' every 32 tiers containing a local charge-to-current amplifier and a segment switch on each vertical bitline, so a 1-2 fF cell sees only its 32-tier segment and one base sense amp serves the whole column.
why: Lets Cs drop ~3x and tiers grow 10x without growing periphery (fact 7: ~49% of die), so die cost holds flat at 10x bits.

title: Spin-crossover molecular tiers with room-temperature-straddling hysteresis loops
idea: Thermal hysteresis: Fe(II)-triazole spin-crossover films whose 30-40 K hysteresis loop is engineered to straddle 20-60 C hold either the high-spin or low-spin state with no power. A heater pulse writes high-spin, a field pulse writes low-spin, and the ~10% dielectric or resistance change is the read. The films can be evaporated at <200 C, so many cheap tiers fit in BEOL.
why: Gives non-volatile tiers from molecules with no critical minerals (resource axis, fact 2); claim very low capital per tier. Speed and endurance are unproven.

title: Matrix Semiconductor's write-once 3D ROM as a weights tier
idea: Matrix Semiconductor's 8-deck antifuse crosspoint (2001) failed because nobody wanted write-once storage. LLM inference does: burn model weights into a stack of antifuse decks over the accelerator's periphery, read in tens of ns. The weights no longer occupy DRAM, which then holds only KV cache and activations.
why: Does DRAM's job with less DRAM: weights are ~50-80% of inference memory, written once at ~10x DRAM's bits per mm2, with no refresh.

title: Roll a 2D array film into a multi-turn scroll
idea: Turn area into tiers by rolling instead of stacking: fabricate a thin-film oxide DRAM array on a strained bilayer membrane with the existing mask set, then use one added release mask so the film self-rolls into a 10-30 turn Swiss roll, with turns connected through contacts at the scroll edge.
why: Density and 3D cost (facts 2,4): 10-30x bits per footprint without per-tier processing; rolled-up nanomembrane capacitors already exist.

title: Embargoed Soviet engineer prints arrays with mask-free laser interference
idea: With no EUV and no mask shop, the Soviet engineer treats the array as a crystal lattice. A 4-beam 193 nm immersion interference exposure prints the whole field's periodic hole and line grid without a mask, spacer doubling takes it to ~20 nm pitch, and one coarse KrF trim mask cuts mats and edges.
why: Takes the 3-5 array EUV layers off: a ~$5M interference tool replaces a $200M+ scanner for the most repeated layers (Fact 4, capital).

title: Downhole-200C Ga2O3 vertical gain-cell tiers become refresh-free at room temperature
idea: Design the cell for a 200 C oil-well logging tool: a capacitor-less 2T gain cell whose write and read transistors are vertical beta-Ga2O3 (4.8 eV bandgap) pillars at 4F2, stacked 8-16 tiers over CMOS by low-temperature ALD. A cell qualified to hold charge 10 ms at 200 C holds it for many minutes at 85 C, so the same array ships to datacenters with refresh essentially gone.
why: Attacks the leakage tail and refresh (fact 3) and the capacitor wall (fact 1); recovers 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth, and 4F2 vertical stacking gives ~3-8x bits per mm2.

title: Leaky flash: 3D NAND fabs build volatile charge-trap DRAM
idea: Adapted from 3D NAND (already ~$0.05/GB): keep the 200+ tier charge-trap string but thin the tunnel oxide to ~1.5 nm direct-tunneling so writes take ~10-50 ns at ~4 V, retention drops to ~1 s and endurance rises beyond 10^12; read through NAND page buffers and refresh each second, fronted by an SRAM cache.
why: Inherits NAND's per-bit cost (~100x below DRAM) and U.S.-buildable toolsets; trade-offs: 100-300 ns page-random reads and page-granular access.

title: AlScN wurtzite ferrodiode makes self-rectifying 3D ferroelectric cross-points
idea: Polarization-modulated Schottky barrier: in CMOS-compatible ferroelectric AlScN, deposited at ≤400 C, switching polarization raises or lowers the interface barrier. Each cell is therefore a non-volatile diode that both stores and rectifies, so selector-free cross-point tiers stack over logic.
why: Gives non-volatile 4F2 stacked arrays with very long retention and no access transistor (facts 2 and 4); claim 4-8 tiers in BEOL over periphery.

title: Micro-mat activation with sub-wordline drivers built into each tier
idea: IFR: 'an activate opens only the bytes requested.' Backward: tile each 3D tier into 4 kb micro-mats and build an oxide-semiconductor sub-wordline driver inside the tier at each mat edge, so the global wordline only steers a local driver and one ACT energizes 512 bits instead of 8 kB.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): ~16x less activate energy, taking random reads from ~5.9 pJ toward ~0.5-1 pJ per useful bit.

title: Factory-programmed charge-trap back-gates permanently stiffen every tier
idea: Po: the transistor is told once, forever, to stay off. Give each tier's lateral access transistors a buried ONO charge-trap back-gate programmed once at final test to shift Vt by about +0.8 V, cutting subthreshold leakage ~1e8x while a boosted front gate restores on-current; no negative wordline generator is needed.
why: Refresh: removes the subthreshold tail with one-time programming (no endurance concern) and trims tier-to-tier Vt spread; GIDL handled with a lightly doped drain.

title: Overlay-free bonded capacitor extension through a sub-pitch nanorod carpet
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation: split the capacitor across two wafers, and split the bond interface into a random carpet of 8 nm TiN-cored, high-k-coated nanorods at 1/4 cell pitch embedded in a common plate. When this wafer is bonded onto the array wafer's isolated storage pads, each pad statistically catches ~10 rod tips while the pad gap (> rod diameter) prevents bridging, so no cell-pitch overlay is needed.
why: Fact 1: adds ~3-5 fF per cell from an independently made wafer (doubling Cs without deeper etch) and decouples capacitor fab from transistor fab (capital, U.S. second source).

title: Boron-doped etch-stop superlattice replaces SiGe for lateral 3D DRAM
idea: Build the 3D DRAM tier stack as single-crystal Si epitaxy with alternating heavily boron-doped layers (US borate supply) instead of Si/SiGe, then remove the p++ layers with a dopant-selective HNA-type wet etch to open lateral capacitor and channel cavities, using no germanium.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2) and scarce resources: germanium is largely China-sourced; Si/Si:B has near-zero lattice mismatch, so less strain and more (100+) tiers, all domestic.

title: Selectron-style binary-coded tier selection replaces staircase contacts
idea: Revive RCA's Selectron, whose grid bars picked one eyelet by binary coincidence: at each mat edge every tier's wordline passes through log2(N) series select transistors whose thresholds are binary-coded per tier with log2(N) chop masks (the mask-halving trick already used for staircases), so 7 complementary vertical select-gate pairs choose one of 128 tiers. Fourteen contacts replace 128 staircase landings.
why: Facts 2, 4 and 7: staircase area and contact count scale as log2(N) instead of N, making 100+ tier 3D DRAM affordable in area and mask count.

title: Film-projector token ring replaces decoders for CMOS-free tiles
idea: Adapted from film projectors that advance one frame per sprocket pulse: each 1 Mb tile selects rows with a token passed along an in-array oxide-TFT shift register and streams columns out a shift-register row buffer, so the tile has no address decoders and can be built entirely from TFTs on glass or foil.
why: Periphery shrinks from ~49% of die to ~5% (fact 7) and CMOS leaves the array substrate, enabling panel- or roll-built memory near $0.1/GB; trade-off: sequential row walks (~1 us worst case) hidden by a cache.

title: Cell-to-pack memory: unsingulated DRAM wafers bonded onto compute wafers
idea: Like EV cell-to-pack removing the module layer, skip die singulation, packages and DIMMs: wafer-bond whole yield-mapped DRAM wafers (with spare-tile rerouting) onto whole compute wafers so memory meets compute through millions of bonds at full wafer scale.
why: HBM TSV tax and data movement (facts 5, 6): removes TSVs, interposer and package; claims ~3x area efficiency vs HBM and ~100 TB/s per wafer pair.

title: Delta-modulation encoding for AI tensors in error-prone 3D strings
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1946 delta modulation: store KV-cache and activation sequences as 1-bit delta streams along the token axis across vertical tiers, so each cell's bit is worth one small step and a 1% cell BER adds only ~1% amplitude noise; the controller integrates on read.
why: Facts 1 and 5: lets marginal ~2 fF cells hold AI working sets; ~3x denser cells outweigh the ~1.5-2x bit overhead of delta coding for correlated tensors.

title: Bonded nonvolatile shadow tier dumps idle banks before power-off
idea: Po: memory that sleeps with its eyes shut. Pair each DRAM tier with a hybrid-bonded thick-oxide charge-trap shadow tier sharing its vertical bitlines, so an idle bank copies out in parallel in ~10 us and is power-gated; dumps are rate-limited to one per bank per 5 minutes, so 1e6-cycle endurance lasts ~10 years.
why: Refresh and idle power to zero for idle banks (16-33% of idle power, fact 3) without slowing active banks.

title: Magnify capacitor sidewall area 2.5x with corrugated superlattice mold
idea: Deposit the capacitor mold as an alternating SiN/SiO2 (or Si/SiGe) superlattice, etch the hole, then selectively recess every other layer, so the pillar sidewall becomes a corrugated bellows that the ALD electrode and dielectric coat conformally.
why: Charge wall: about 2.5x more electrode area, and so Cs, at the same AR of 60-75. This could avoid the jump to AR 115.

title: Biologist's cortical minicolumns: 16-cell bitlines with private sense amps
idea: The cortex scales by repeating short minicolumns. Split the 3D array into 16-32-cell local bitlines; a 4x4 bundle of them is muxed in the array tier onto one hybrid bond to a sense amp in a CMOS wafer below.
why: Bitline capacitance falls to ~1-2 fF, so at the same signal margin Cs can drop from ~5 fF to ~1 fF. That removes the 60-75:1 capacitor (Fact 1) and enables shallow 3D tiers.

title: IBM Josephson lesson: run DRAM at 77 K, not superconducting
idea: IBM's 1980s Josephson computer program died largely for lack of a dense cryogenic memory. Instead of superconducting memory, run 3D DRAM tiers at liquid-nitrogen temperature. Access-transistor leakage drops by orders of magnitude, so retention stretches to hours, and the capacitor can shrink about 10x.
why: Removes refresh (fact 3) and the charge wall (fact 1), allowing short, cheap capacitors in many tiers. LN2 cooling avoids helium.

title: Milestone prize ladder for printed DRAM foils reaching $1/GB
idea: Fund a federal prize ladder paid on independent testing: about $10M for a 1 Gb printed foil with 64 ms retention, $50M for under-100 ns access with 1e15-cycle endurance, and $200M for packaged modules under $1/GB built on U.S. R2R lines.
why: Targets the physics gates (retention, speed, endurance) rather than picking a technology, pulling many teams into the area-is-cheap regime that bypasses EUV (fact 4) and fab capital; money flows only on measured results.

title: Overbuild 120 tiers, fuse to 100: tier-level sparing
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial or excessive action: deliberately deposit ~20% more tiers than the product needs, add a per-block tier-remap register, and e-fuse out any tier that fails test (shorts, Vt outliers, weak capacitors). The process window can then be loosened (faster deposition, cheaper precursors) because whole-tier defects become yield-neutral.
why: Fact 2: turns compounding tier loss (0.99^100 ~ 37% yield) into >90% die yield, cutting 3D cost per bit ~2x at a fixed defect density.

title: Copper spiral coils link stacked dies wirelessly instead of TSVs
idea: Pattern 20-40 um Cu inductor coils by lift-off or plating on each thinned memory die and stack the dies with adhesive; inductive coupling carries Gb/s data per coil pair through 4-8 dies, while power arrives through a few coarse TSVs or edge wires.
why: Cuts the HBM TSV tax (fact 6): less keep-out area and TSV yield loss, and adhesive stacking replaces fine-pitch bonding; coils are single-mask university builds.

title: Read-restore 3T gain cell: every read is a refresh
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: add a p-type third transistor whose gate is the precharged read bitline and whose channel links the storage gate to a restore rail. When a stored 1 pulls the read bitline low, the feedback device turns on and tops the storage node back up; a stored 0 leaves the bitline high and the device off.
why: Fact 3: accessed rows refresh themselves, so explicit refresh covers only cold rows (~50-90% fewer refresh operations for typical access patterns); no capacitor.

title: Minify tier thickness to 6 nm for 1000-tier atomic stacks
idea: Grow alternating MOCVD 2D-semiconductor channel sheets (MoS2 or WSe2, about 1 nm) and hBN/oxide spacers (about 5 nm) so each tier is 6 nm and 1000 tiers fit in a 6 um stack. Gain-cell storage nodes are gated by shared vertical gate holes etched once per 100-tier deck, as in 3D NAND.
why: 3D break-even (26+ tiers): goes 40x past it at a stack height that an etcher can already reach; the wide bandgap of 2D channels also cuts leakage, so refresh could fall by more than 100x.

title: Marquetry slab: reconstituted wafer of harvested partial-good banks
idea: Like inlaid marquetry made from offcuts, dice partially failing mature DRAM dies along bank boundaries, inlay the good banks into a pocketed reconstituted wafer on existing fan-out lines, and wire them with one coarse RDL into a wafer-scale memory slab with a routing table.
why: Recovers bits from scrapped dies (~5-15% of output) and builds large capacity slabs with no new fab, lowering scarce-resource use per usable bit.

title: Thermally trimmed wafer distortion for cell-pitch wafer-to-wafer bonding
idea: TRIZ #37 Thermal expansion: map both wafers' in-plane distortion, then heat the top-wafer bond chuck with a zoned IR array so each region expands by exactly the ppm needed just before contact. Residual overlay falls from ~100 nm to <20 nm, enough to bond a separately built capacitor wafer onto ~40 nm-pitch storage pads.
why: Fact 1 and 4: makes capacitor fab and transistor fab separable (different tools, sites, even companies), each with a simpler, cheaper flow.

title: Jellyroll-wound memory ribbon: battery winding replaces tier deposition
idea: Borrowing the lithium-ion jellyroll, fabricate a long released ribbon (thin polyimide on a sacrificial carrier) carrying one tier of low-temperature thin-film transistors and planar MIM capacitors, then wind it on a mandrel so every turn becomes a tier. Tier-to-tier and tier-to-logic contacts run through edge tabs exactly like battery current collectors, landing on a radial bus bonded to the CMOS base.
why: 3D tier count and capital (facts 2, 4): one patterning pass per ribbon yields 100+ effective tiers by winding instead of 100 deposition/etch cycles; claims ~10x lower capex per tier, accepting low per-tier density.

title: Laser-crystallized silicon tiers stacked in BEOL above logic
idea: Inverts 'crystalline access transistors require front-end epitaxy.' Deposit amorphous Si on each tier and crystallize it with an excimer-laser super-lateral-growth pulse whose heat stays in the top ~100 nm, building dozens of near-crystalline Si access-transistor tiers over finished logic with Si only.
why: Facts 2 and 7: array tiers over the periphery with no In/Ga oxides, using display-industry laser tools and no EUV.

title: Satellite-lot nanoimprint tiers: periodic arrays without excimer or EUV
idea: Space programs build memory in lots too small to amortize EUV, and EUV and ArF sources consume neon, helium, krypton or argon; a DRAM array layer is a perfectly periodic line or hole lattice, so print it by jet-and-flash nanoimprint cured with UV LEDs and write only the small non-periodic periphery with a multi-beam electron writer. Every tier reuses the same template, and transfer etches run on HBr/O2 chemistry with no argon dilution.
why: Removes 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4) and the neon/helium supply risk; template ~10x cheaper than an EUV mask set and tool capex ~$30M vs $200M+.

title: Minify DRAM die to 0.5 mm2 confetti, self-assembled onto logic
idea: Make DRAM as tiny 0.5 mm2 micro-dies, whose small area gives near-100% yield, and deposit thousands at once onto logic wafers by fluidic self-assembly into shaped receptor wells, followed by hybrid bonding.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield: avoids the 20-30% stack yield loss and the 3x area per bit, with a microLED-style mass-transfer cost.

title: Alien Technology's fluidic self-assembly for replaceable DRAM mat chiplets
idea: Alien Technology's fluidic self-assembly (FSA) of tiny dies into shaped wells failed commercially for RFID. Make DRAM as 0.5 mm 'mat chiplets' that self-assemble into receptor wells on a periphery wafer and attach with low-melt solder. Bad chiplets are melted out and replaced, and at end of life all chiplets are released in a hot bath for retest and reuse.
why: Tiny chiplets yield ~99% (fact 4 capital), the periphery wafer can use an older US node (fact 7), and repair and recycling work at the chiplet level.

title: Coin-sorter assembly: fluidic self-assembly of DRAM micro-chiplets onto logic
idea: Like coin sorters dropping coins into shaped slots, agitate 300 um shape-keyed mature-node DRAM micro-chiplets in fluid over a logic wafer with matching receptor wells so they fall in and lock, then planarize and connect them with one RDL, placing thousands per minute.
why: Puts memory directly over compute using cheap mature dies, cutting data-movement energy (fact 5) and pick-and-place capex; fluidic self-assembly is proven for RFID and microLED.

title: Eliminate open-bitline dummy edge mats: self-referenced double sampling
idea: Replace reference-from-neighbour-mat sensing with a sense amp that samples its own bitline before and after charge sharing on a small on-SA capacitor, so the half-used dummy mats at array edges disappear.
why: Periphery/area: edge dummy mats waste ~3-5% of array area in open-bitline 6F2/4F2 designs; also gives better offset cancellation.

title: Dendritic bitline trees with spine amplifiers at every branch
idea: Replace long flat bitlines with a neuron-like dendritic tree in the 3D stack: each 8-cell twig joins its branch through a one-transistor oxide-TFT charge-transfer preamp at the branch point (an active dendritic conductance), so a cell only ever charges ~5-10 fF of twig instead of ~60 fF of bitline.
why: Capacitor charge wall: ~6x better Cs/CBL lets 1 fF capacitors (AR ~15:1) still give >=100 mV signal, removing the need for AR 115 or k 70.

title: Hotel-keycard micro-rows: coincident gating opens only 64 bits
idea: Like a keycard that opens one room instead of the whole floor, give each 3D DRAM cell a series pair of access gates, the tier wordline plus a vertical column-group select, so an activation opens only the 64 cells at the intersection rather than an 8 Kb page, and only those bitlines swing and restore.
why: Destructive read and overfetch (fact 8): 128x overfetch falls to ~1x, so activate-plus-restore energy per useful bit claims >10x lower (5.9 pJ toward <0.5 pJ).

title: Boron nitride monolayers shrink inter-tier spacers to three nanometers
idea: Replace the 20-30 nm SiO2 spacer between 3D-DRAM tiers with 2-3 layers of hexagonal BN (6 eV gap, pinhole-free van der Waals insulator) grown on a sacrificial template and transferred or directly grown by low-temperature plasma CVD, cutting tier pitch from ~60 nm to ~35 nm.
why: Hole-etch depth, not tier count, caps 3D DRAM (facts 1, 2); 1.7x more tiers in the same ~6 um stack reaches the 26-tier breakeven at a far lower etch aspect ratio.

title: HFT dual-port cell: capacitor sandwiched between two vertical transistors
idea: High-frequency traders cannot tolerate refresh stalls; build a vertical cell whose capacitor sits between a bottom access transistor on bitline A, owned by a refresh/scrub engine, and a top access transistor on bitline B, owned by the host. Stacking makes the second port free in footprint, so refresh, row-hammer mitigation and ECC scrub run on port A while port B serves traffic.
why: Refresh bandwidth loss of 10-20% (fact 3) and row-hammer mitigation stalls (fact 9) become invisible; deterministic latency and ~10-20% more usable bandwidth per die.

title: 77 K cryogenic DRAM stacks with tenfold smaller capacitors
idea: [Box: small planar MIM | Si or poly-Si FET | charge-share SA | many-tier monolithic | Si | relaxed DUV] Run memory racks at liquid-nitrogen temperature where leakage falls by 1e4 or more and retention climbs to minutes; cells use 0.5-1 fF low-AR capacitors and leakier thin-film transistors, so tiers stack cheaply.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1), refresh (fact 3) and wire energy (fact 5, Cu resistance ~6x lower): near-zero refresh, simple cells; cooling cost amortized in AI datacenters.

title: HP's The Machine fixed: pooled memory racks with a refurbishment loop
idea: HPE's The Machine died betting on an unready memristor. Build the same memory-centric fabric with today's DRAM in CXL-attached pooled racks, sold as a service. Modules are hot-swapped, tested, refurbished and redeployed to lower tiers instead of retiring with the server.
why: Pooling cuts stranded DRAM (often 20-40% unused per server), and refurbishment roughly doubles module life, raising usable supply without new fabs.

title: Esaki tunnel-diode bistable cells as stackable two-terminal static RAM
idea: Revive 1960s tunnel-diode memories: a BEOL-grown interband tunnel diode (oxide or 2D heterojunction) in series with a thin-film load has two stable operating points held by a shared standby-bias line, and 4-8 such decks stack as crosspoint static memory read by small current pulses.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor and no refresh; two-terminal decks dodge the 3D transistor blocker, viable if peak-to-valley ratio >10 keeps standby below DRAM refresh power.

title: Monolayer MoS2 channel tiers stacked at 20 nm pitch
idea: Quantum confinement: atomically thin MoS2 channels, MOCVD-grown at <450 C, have a ~2 eV confined bandgap that suppresses off-state tunneling and thermionic leakage about 1000x versus silicon. Because each channel is only 0.7 nm thick, tiers can stack at ~20 nm pitch, which makes 50+ tiers practical.
why: Shrinks tier pitch and leakage at once (facts 2 and 3); claim 3D break-even reached at lower stack height and 10x longer retention.

title: Glass-panel DRAM self-aligned by backside exposure
idea: Build oxide-semiconductor DRAM tiers on large glass panels and expose the photoresist through the glass from below, so the opaque buried wordlines act as the mask for the channel/source-drain pattern above them; the only added mask is the panel contact opening.
why: Capital and litho (fact 4): panel area is ~10x a 300 mm wafer, display fabs have spare capacity, and self-alignment removes a critical overlay step.

title: Grid surge-arrester zinc-oxide varistors select crossbar DRAM capacitors
idea: Adapted from power-grid metal-oxide surge arresters, whose ZnO grain boundaries conduct ~10^10x more above a knee voltage: stack 8 decks of 1-selector-1-capacitor crossbars where a nanograin ZnO-Bi2O3 varistor film isolates each capacitor below half-select voltage, 2 masks per deck.
why: Transistor-free crossbar decks reach ~4F2/8 per bit at a fraction of DRAM process cost, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-offs: ~ms retention needing aggressive refresh, high write voltages.

title: MLCC-in-a-cell: forty-plate interdigitated capacitor per bit
idea: Under 400 C, ALD forty alternating Ru and TiN plates separated by 4 nm ZrO2 (crystalline as deposited at about 275 C). Selectively recess Ru on one hole sidewall and TiN on the other so each cell's two contacts tie to alternating plates, like an MLCC termination.
why: Fact 1: about 5 fF in a 40x40 nm footprint at about 9:1 AR instead of 75:1; the capacitor scales by plate count, not etch depth.

title: Freestanding single-crystal SrTiO3 membranes bonded as planar DRAM capacitors
idea: [Box: paraelectric perovskite charge | Si 4F2 VCT | charge-share SA | low-temperature membrane bonding | SrTiO3 donor wafer | epitaxy + water-soluble Sr3Al2O6 release] Grow epitaxial SrRuO3/SrTiO3 at ~700 C on a donor, free it by dissolving a Sr3Al2O6 sacrificial layer, and bond the membrane onto the finished transistor array below 300 C, then pattern planar or <=10:1 capacitors with k~150-300. The crystal's thermal budget never touches the access transistor or lower tiers.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): k~150+ reaches 5 fF at AR<10 instead of 60-75:1, deleting the deepest etch; also makes a capacitor that can sit on any 3D tier.

title: Skyscraper architect's sky lobbies: periphery tiers every 32 floors
idea: Tall towers use sky lobbies so no elevator runs the full height. Every 32 array tiers, insert a laser-crystallized Si or oxide CMOS 'lobby' tier holding local tier decoders and wordline drivers. Global lines only reach lobbies, and each staircase spans just 32 steps.
why: Removes the height limit on 3D DRAM (Fact 2) and shrinks staircase and periphery area (Fact 7), toward 128+ tiers.

title: Termite-mound thermosiphon chimneys through the DRAM stack
idea: Termite mounds cool themselves with passive convection chimneys; etch a sparse grid of sealed ~20 um chimneys through a 16-24 high bonded DRAM stack, partly filled with a dielectric working fluid that boils near the hot logic tier and condenses at the lid, pumping heat with no pump.
why: Thermal ceiling on stack height and refresh (facts 3, 6): retention roughly halves per 10 C, so keeping upper tiers ~15 C cooler cuts refresh ~2-3x and allows ~1.5x more tiers per stack within the thermal budget.

title: Magnify bus width 8x on a cheap glass interposer
idea: Place four bare commodity LPDDR dies side by side on a panel-made glass interposer with 2 um lines, giving a 1024-bit bus to an FPGA or ASIC without TSVs or a silicon interposer, built through glass-panel vendors for about $300k.
why: HBM TSV tax: HBM-like bandwidth from LPDDR bits, without HBM's 3x wafer area per bit or stack yield loss.

title: Array-only wafers bonded to U.S. mature-node periphery wafers
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: pull all periphery (sense amps, decoders, charge pumps, I/O) off the DRAM wafer onto a 28-40 nm logic wafer from a U.S. foundry, then wafer-to-wafer hybrid bond at ~1 um pitch. The DRAM fab runs only the array flow, so its EUV and high-AR tools spend all their time on bits.
why: Fact 7 and U.S. manufacturability: array efficiency rises from ~51% to ~85% of die area (~1.6x bits per array wafer) and roughly half the process steps move to existing U.S. fabs.

title: Sense amps flipped beneath array, one per 128-cell bitline
idea: Move sense amplifiers from mat edges to a logic wafer hybrid-bonded underneath, with one ~0.4 um-pitch bond per 128-cell bitline segment (staggered so pads fit), giving every short bitline its own SA directly below. Bitline capacitance falls ~6-8x versus 1k-cell bitlines, so a ~1 fF capacitor delivers today's signal.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): capacitor AR can fall from 60-75:1 to ~10-15:1, removing the hardest etch; shorter bitlines also cut sensing energy and latency.

title: Vertical bucket-brigade columns move charge to one sense amp
idea: Po: the bits move, the sense amp stays. Make each 3D column a vertical charge-coupled device whose tiers are three-phase clocked gate electrodes; charge packets shift down the pillar to a single sense amp at the bottom, with no per-cell access transistor or bitline contact.
why: Facts 2 and 7: no lateral transistor per cell and ~1 sense amp per 100+ bits; serial latency fits sequential AI weight streaming, not random access.

title: Stilts: low-temperature wordline drivers built above the array, not beside it
idea: Stilts lift a house over its plot: build the sub-wordline drivers and column-select switches as <400 C oxide-semiconductor or laser-annealed poly-Si transistors in the BEOL directly over the cell array, connected down by vias, while Si sense amps and I/O stay below. Mat-edge driver stripes disappear, and externally it is still a standard DDR5 die.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7): removes ~15-20% of die area (driver and column-select stripes), about 20% more bits per wafer.

title: Titanium angle-evaporation forms self-aligned half-gates on pillar arrays
idea: Tilt the wafer 60-75 degrees in an e-beam evaporator so Ti lands only on one face and a set height band of each pillar (neighbors shadow the rest), then nitride it; rotating between evaporations writes wordlines and contacts at self-aligned heights with no lithography.
why: Shadow-defined wordlines on 4F2 pillars remove critical masks (fact 4) and set gate length by geometry, and the gate-free face lowers GIDL (fact 3); a tilt-stage evaporator is ubiquitous in university fabs.

title: Sodium-ion electret back-gates set each tier's threshold without wiring
idea: Implant a controlled Na+ dose into the buried oxide beneath each tier of p-channel lateral access transistors, drift it to the BOX top in a one-time field anneal, then seal it with SiN; the frozen charge acts as a permanent back-gate bias raising |Vt| by ~0.3 V.
why: Cuts the access-transistor leakage tail (fact 3) ~10x, stretching refresh intervals, with no negative wordline pump or per-tier back-gate contacts that would add staircase and periphery area (fact 7).

title: Pulse electroplating grows a 200-layer wordline stack in one bath
idea: Borrowed from compositionally modulated multilayer electroplating: plate a 200-period Cu/Ni superlattice from one bath by switching potential, selectively recess one metal and backfill oxide, forming the 3D wordline stack without CVD tungsten.
why: Plating costs ~1/100 of CVD/ALD per layer and avoids tungsten (China ~80%); stack deposition cost ~-95%; trade-offs: barrier liners, uniformity at the wafer edge.

title: Deinococcus genome repair: vertical erasure codes span the tiers
idea: Deinococcus radiodurans rebuilds shattered genomes from overlapping copies; stripe each word across 16 tiers of a vertical column plus 4 parity tiers (Reed-Solomon over tiers), so a whole tier lost to 125 C bond voiding, contact drift or a wordline open is corrected on the fly.
why: High-temperature 10-yr life in 3D stacks is dominated by tier-correlated wear-out that per-word ECC cannot fix; vertical erasure coding at 25% overhead tolerates multiple full-tier failures.

title: Solar-cell economics: metal-assisted wet etching drills AR-200 capacitor holes
idea: Solar wafer makers texture silicon for cents with metal-assisted chemical etching; for DRAM, imprint a silver or platinum catalyst mesh and etch in HF/H2O2 at room temperature, which drills straight silicon holes at AR 200:1 with no plasma, no argon and no helium-cooled chuck. Line the holes with ALD electrode and high-k to form deep trench capacitors in each array tier.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): AR 200 vs 60-75 gives ~2.5x Cs or a 2.5x smaller footprint, and the most expensive plasma etch and its rare gases are removed.

title: Eliminate CMP before bonding: in-vacuum atomic diffusion bonding
idea: Stack tiers by sputtering a few nm of Ti or Au-free metal onto both surfaces in the same vacuum and pressing them together at room temperature (atomic diffusion bonding), with no CMP to 0.5 nm roughness and no wet surface activation.
why: Water: hybrid bonding's CMP plus megasonic clean is repeated per bonded tier; vacuum bonding is dry, cutting bonding water ~10x and enabling cheaper multi-tier stacks.

title: Alien without lithography grows pores: anodized-alumina capacitor forest
idea: An alien that never invented lithography would grow the array. Anodize a 3-5 um sputtered Al film over CMOS so hexagonal self-ordered pores form at 25-60 nm pitch and >100:1 aspect ratio. Imprinted dimples at landing sites pin each pore over its transistor, and the pores are lined by ALD to become coaxial capacitors.
why: Reaches the AR ~115 that Fact 1 calls for with a wet electrochemical step instead of high-AR plasma etch; the capacitor layer needs no critical masks.

title: Mirror-tier pairs share one horizontal bitline sheet
idea: Limit: half a metal layer per tier. Build tiers as mirrored pairs around a single horizontal bitline plane, with cells above and below contacting the same bitline. This halves bitline layers and cuts tier pitch about 25%.
why: Fact 2: more tiers per micron of stack height and fewer deposition/etch layers per bit, about 1.3x density per stack height.

title: Sunflower phyllotaxis pillar layout starves row-hammer aggressors
idea: Place vertical-channel cells in each mat on a golden-angle (137.5 deg) Fibonacci spiral tiling with wordlines following the parastichy spirals; because neighbours along irrational spiral directions never align, no victim has a single dominant parallel aggressor and coupling is split over 8+ weak neighbours, as sunflower seeds pack without aligned gaps.
why: Row hammer (~1k activations): spreading coupling could raise the hammer threshold ~4-8x and remove aggressor-counting logic, at near-optimal packing density.

title: Ten-electron quantum-dot storage node read by a single-electron transistor
idea: Jump down to the electron count: store a bit as ~10 electrons on a 3-nm silicon quantum dot behind an engineered double tunnel barrier, whose Coulomb blockade gives ms-to-s retention. An adjacent single-electron transistor reads it, its current swinging fully per electron, so cell capacitance is ~1 aF instead of 5 fF.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) by trading charge quantity for charge sensitivity: ~1000x less stored charge, enabling 3D cells under 20 nm.

title: Arsenal conversion: retool legacy 3D-NAND lines for vertical oxide DRAM
idea: Like WWII car plants converted to bombers, fund conversion of 48-96-layer 3D NAND lines, which need no EUV and already own deep-hole etch and staircase tools, to make vertical-string oxide-channel gain-cell DRAM under a Defense Production Act Title III style program with offtake guarantees.
why: Fastest route to 3D DRAM tiers (fact 2) without a $15B, 3-5 year fab; reuses depreciated deep-etch capacity and policy can unlock it in months.

title: Array sandwiched between two CMOS wafers: double-sided periphery
idea: Jump from one die face to a wafer-pair sandwich: hybrid-bond a CMOS wafer to both the top and the bottom of a thinned memory-array wafer, with wordline drivers on one side and sense amps on the other. That doubles the periphery area under the array and allows mats half as large with shorter lines.
why: Periphery is 49% of the die (fact 7): moving all of it off the array plane approaches ~90% array efficiency, ~1.7x bits per array-wafer area.

title: Plateless bridge capacitor stores one bit between twin nodes
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: merge the two capacitors of a twin cell into one capacitor whose two electrodes are both storage nodes, each reached by its own access transistor on complementary bitlines, with no common plate. Writing puts +V/-V across the single capacitor and the sense amp sees the full differential charge.
why: Fact 1 and 10: ~2x signal per fF lets Cs halve or VARY drop ~30%; deleting the plate layer saves a deposition and contact module.

title: Etched-anodized aluminum foil substrate is the shared capacitor plate
idea: Borrow the electrolytic-capacitor recipe for the array substrate: tunnel-etch aluminum foil for ~50x surface area, anodize ~10 nm of Al2O3, then print each cell's conductive-polymer storage electrode and oxide TFT on top, with the foil itself as common plate, ground shield and heat spreader.
why: Low-voltage electrolytic foils already exceed ~10 uF/cm^2, i.e. ~100+ fF per um^2, so charge is abundant (fact 1) on a substrate made today by the kilometre, with anodization as a cheap wet R2R step.

title: Rubik's cube: transposable 3D cell with orthogonal row and column access
idea: A Rubik's cube twists along either axis: each storage node connects to two access transistors in different tiers, a lower one gated by an X-wordline onto Y-bitlines and an upper one gated by a Y-wordline onto X-bitlines. The array can open a row or a column, so matrix transposes and column-wise tensor reads need no overfetch.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) and data movement (fact 5): claim 2-4x less energy per useful bit on transposed or strided AI access, at ~1.3x cell area that tiers absorb.

title: Chemically coded tier metals replace staircase contacts
idea: Po: the stack has no staircase. Build each tier's wordline from a distinct tungsten-free metal/liner pair (Mo, Ru, Co, TiN with unique etch-stop liners) so a contact etch stops on the target tier by chemistry; combined with binary chop etches, 64 tiers are contacted with ~6 masks in a single small contact field.
why: Facts 2/4: staircase area (~5-10% of die) and trim steps scale with tiers; chemical coding makes contact cost logarithmic and avoids tungsten (China ~80%).

title: Laser-written cube-face bus replaces HBM through-silicon vias
idea: IFR: 'the stack has full bandwidth and no TSVs.' Backward: stack DRAM dies with all I/O routed to one edge, mold the stack, polish that face, and laser-direct-write then electroplate ~2,000 copper lines at 5 um pitch down the cube face to the base die.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): recovers TSV keep-out area and TSV-related yield loss, part of HBM's ~3x area per bit and 20-30% yield penalty.

title: Irvine Sensors edge-stack revived: printed sidewall buses instead of TSVs
idea: Irvine Sensors' 1990s 'loaf-of-bread' cubes routed signals to die edges and metallized the stack's side, but died on thinning yield and coarse wiring. Route each DRAM die's I/O to edge pads, stack the dies, polish the side, and laser-direct-write or aerosol-print fine-pitch copper buses down the sidewall. No TSV pierces the array.
why: Removes the TSV area and yield tax (fact 6). Edge buses at 10 um pitch carry wide I/O. Claims ~2x bits per wafer area vs HBM.

title: TSV-free HBM: ThruChip inductive links plus power-only vias
idea: HMC's power-hungry SerDes and Keio's ThruChip inductive-coupling interface both stalled, and HBM won while paying a large TSV tax. Stack DRAM dies with on-die spiral coils carrying data over near-field links (~0.1 pJ/bit). Keep only a sparse ring of large power TSVs at the die edge, so about 90% of TSVs and their keep-out zones disappear.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax (fact 6: 3x wafer area per bit, 20-30% yield loss). Targets ~1.5x area per bit and recovers most of the yield loss.

title: Keep the SiGe layers: superlattice wells become floating-body storage
idea: [Box: holes in a SiGe quantum well | lateral Si nanosheet FET | current sense | monolithic Si/SiGe superlattice | Si | epitaxy-defined layers, ArF slits] Normally the SiGe in a 3D-DRAM superlattice is sacrificial; instead grade each sheet as Si channel / thin SiGe well / Si so the valence-band offset traps holes as a capacitorless storage node under each lateral gate.
why: 3D blockers (fact 2): no lateral capacitor, ~3x shorter cell; all critical dimensions set by epitaxy thickness.

title: Photographic contact print: Talbot self-imaging for periodic cell arrays
idea: Use displacement Talbot lithography, a contact-print-like method exploiting self-imaging of periodic masks, to expose dense hexagonal capacitor or channel arrays below 100 nm pitch with mature UV sources, then spacer pitch-split to ~40 nm.
why: Array layers are perfectly periodic, exactly Talbot's sweet spot; replaces immersion/EUV array exposures (fact 4) with ~$1-3M tools.

title: Binary-coded vertical tier select replaces staircase contacts
idea: Give each tier a tiny thin-film decoder hard-wired to its own tier number and run only log2(N) true/complement address rods vertically through the stack, so selecting one of 128 tiers needs 14 rods instead of a 128-step staircase with 128 contacts.
why: Staircase area and contact etch grow O(N) with layer count while decoding grows O(log N), so periphery area (fact 7) and etch steps stop scaling with tiers, making 100+ tier 3D DRAM (fact 2) area-viable.

title: Per-tier thin-film decoders replace 3D DRAM wordline staircases
idea: [Box: lateral 1T1C | IGZO lateral FET | conventional SA | monolithic 3D tiers | Si | same ALD IGZO forms a decoder in each tier] Build a tiny IGZO decoder at the array edge of every tier that listens to a shared vertical bundle of log2(N) tier-address lines plus one wordline-drive line, so N tiers need ~log2(N)+k vertical contacts instead of an N-step staircase.
why: 3D break-even at 26+ tiers (fact 2) is eroded by staircase area and trim-etch steps; removing the staircase saves ~5-10% die area and dozens of process steps at 64+ tiers.
